title: Command Reports Failure Through a Status Value Instead of Result
pattern: A state-changing method signals that the command did not take effect through an ordinary return value: `false` from a setter or enqueue, a hand-rolled status enum with an `Ok`/`Success` variant, or a returned state value from which the caller must infer that nothing happened, instead of returning `Result<_, E>`.
why_bad: Failure becomes easy to ignore: a `bool` or custom enum is not `#[must_use]` like `Result`, cannot be propagated with `?`, and carries no reason. Callers end up running commands inside conditions (`if reg.set(..)`, `if mgr.delete_page(..) == ErrorCode::Ok`), which hides the mutation in a predicate, and an implicit signal (an unchanged stock count) is silently misread as success.
detection: A method taking `&mut self` or a `&mut` argument that performs a mutation on one path and returns `bool`, a custom enum containing an `Ok`/`Success`/`None`-like variant alongside error variants, or the post-state value, where the other return value means the requested change was rejected or not performed. Primitive integer status codes and magic sentinel values are a separate criterion.
counterexample: Return values that report an outcome rather than a failure: `HashSet::insert` returning whether the value was new, `HashMap::insert`/`mem::replace` returning the previous value, idempotent ensure-style operations returning whether anything changed, `Option` from a removal whose absence is normal, and `Result<(), E>` itself. C-ABI or `no_std` boundaries that must return status codes.
source: Robert C. Martin, *Clean Code* (2008), Ch. 3 "Command Query Separation" and "Prefer Exceptions to Returning Error Codes"; Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Ch. 7; John Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* (2018), Ch. 4.
